title: Four summaries
hookLine: the world is swept away, has no protector, owns nothing, is a slave to craving

lines: UNDER A TREE IN THE KING'S PARK.
cards: Same sutta, second half. Raṭṭhapāla has left his family's house and is sitting under a tree in the king's park. King Koravya comes out for a stroll, recognizes him, and sits down with real curiosity.
People go forth, the king says, for four reasons: they're old, or sick, or they've lost their money, or they've lost their family. You're young. You're healthy.
Your family is rich and alive. So why? It's a fair question, the kind a friend asks over coffee when you've quit a good job.

teach.h: SWEPT AWAY: AT TWENTY-FIVE, AND AT EIGHTY.
teach.b: Raṭṭhapāla answers with four short sayings he heard from the Buddha, which he calls summaries of the teaching. One: the world is swept away; it does not last. Two: the world has no shelter, no one in charge to protect it.
Three: the world owns nothing; you have to leave everything and go on. Four: the world is never full, never satisfied, a slave to craving. Then he asks the king four questions, one for each.
At twenty-five, how were you at riding, at archery, with a sword? Strong, says the king; sometimes I thought I had no equal. And now?
Now I'm eighty. Sometimes I mean to step one way and my foot goes another. That's the first: swept away.
Do you have an illness? Wind trouble, says the king.

teach.h: NO SHELTER: NOBODY FEELS YOUR PAIN.
teach.b: When it comes, can your ministers and relatives take some of the pain for you? No. I have to feel it all alone.
Second: no shelter. These treasures, will you take them with you? No.

teach.h: OWNS NOTHING: YOU LEAVE IT ALL.
teach.b: Third: you own nothing. And last: if a trusted man came from the east and said there's a rich country there you could conquer, would you? Yes.

teach.h: NEVER FULL: AND BEYOND THE OCEAN?
teach.b: And beyond the ocean? Yes, that too. Fourth: never full.
Raṭṭhapāla doesn't preach at the king. He lets the king's own life answer.
The four summaries aren't meant to make the world look grim. In this sutta they're the reason a young man with everything chose a simpler life, and they're true of kings too.

how: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners reflect regularly on impermanence and the limits of possessions, and teachers use Raṭṭhapāla's four summaries as a short framework for that reflection.

o: four reasons people leave home, like age and loss
four rules a king must follow to rule well
four short sayings on why the world can't satisfy

games.q: each summary and the king's answer: tap the pairs.
p: strong at twenty-five, unsteady at eighty
no one can share his pain
he can't take his treasures with him
he'd conquer beyond the ocean too

s: King Koravya expected people to go forth because of age, sickness, poverty or loss
those were his four reasons, and Raṭṭhapāla had none of them.
Raṭṭhapāla lectures the king without asking him anything
he asks four questions and lets the king's own life answer.
the four summaries are meant to make life look grim
in the sutta they explain why a young man chose a simpler life.

games.q: you're the king. a man arrives from the east: there's a rich country there you could conquer. what does King Koravya say?
games.why: yes, and beyond the ocean too. Raṭṭhapāla: that's the fourth summary. the world is never full.

practice: Choose one of the four, swept away, no shelter, owns nothing, or never full, and let it touch something real: how your body has changed in ten years, a pain only you could feel, a thing you'll leave behind, a want that keeps moving.
Don't push for a feeling. Let the summary be true for a few breaths, and notice what softens.

wordCard.voice: Four summaries. The world is swept away, has no shelter, owns nothing, and is never full. Raṭṭhapāla's answer to a king who asked why he left.

orig.note: Pali: 'the world is swept away; it does not last.' the first of the four summaries.

carryVoice: Your line: the world is swept away. Strong at twenty-five, unsteady at eighty, even for a king. Day four hundred sixty-eight.
